blocks.prompt: The Race Car That Drives Upside Down
blocks.text: A race car does not look like the car your family drives. It sits low and wide. It has big wings on the front and the back. You might think the wings help it fly. They do the opposite. The wings push the car down onto the track. This is called downforce. Downforce presses the tires hard against the road so the car can turn fast without sliding. The tires are smooth with no grooves. Smooth tires grip better when the road is dry. A race car can go faster than a car on the highway, sometimes more than two hundred miles an hour.

blocks.prompt: Answer each question in a full sentence.
items: What do the wings on a race car do?
What is downforce?
Why are race car tires smooth?
answers: they push the car down onto the track
the force that presses the car down
smooth tires grip better on a dry road

blocks.prompt: Everything on a Race Car Has a Job
blocks.text: A race car is built to do one thing better than any other car: get around a track as fast as possible. Everything about it has a job. Take the wings on the front and back. On an airplane, wings lift the plane up into the sky. On a race car, the wings are turned the other way, so instead of lifting the car they press it down. This pressing force is called downforce. It pushes the smooth tires hard against the road, which lets the car take corners at speeds that would send a normal car spinning off the track. Speed also wears out the tires. During a long race, a car stops in the pit lane to get fresh tires. A whole crew swarms the car at once. Each person has one job, and together they can change all four tires in about two seconds. The driver barely has time to breathe before the car is gone again. Races are often won or lost in the pit lane, not just on the track.

answers: get around a track as fast as possible
an airplane wing lifts up, a race car wing presses down
a crew changes all four tires in about two seconds
(inference: a slow or fast pit stop can change who is ahead)

blocks.prompt: Fast Enough to Drive on the Ceiling
blocks.text: A Formula 1 race car is one of the fastest machines a human being can control. It can pass two hundred miles an hour on a straight, then slow down and whip through a tight corner without losing its grip. The secret is downforce. The wings and the shaped floor of the car push air upward, and by pushing air up, they force the car down. At full speed, a Formula 1 car makes so much downforce that, in theory, it could drive along the ceiling of a tunnel upside down and not fall. The air holds it there. That grip has a cost. When the car turns hard, the driver's body is thrown sideways with a force several times stronger than gravity. Drivers train their necks like athletes just to hold their heads up in the corners. Braking is just as violent. The brakes are made of carbon, and they glow orange from the heat as the car slows. The body of the car is a single piece of carbon fiber called a monocoque. It is lighter than steel but far stronger, and it forms a hard shell around the driver. If the car crashes, the shell is built to break apart in pieces that soak up the energy, so the driver walks away. Above the driver's head sits a curved bar called the halo. It looks small, but it has already saved lives by stopping wheels and debris from reaching the person inside.

blocks.prompt: The Track Is a Laboratory
blocks.text: For more than a hundred years, racing has been the place where cars are pushed past every safe limit, and what survives on the track eventually shows up in the cars everyone drives. The earliest races, in the 1890s, ran on ordinary public roads between towns. The machines were slow, loud, and dangerous, and drivers had almost nothing to protect them. Racing has been chasing two goals ever since: go faster, and bring the driver home. Speed came first from bigger engines, but engineers soon learned that shaping the air mattered just as much as raw power. A modern Formula 1 car is really an upside-down wing. Its front wing, rear wing, and carefully sculpted floor bend the passing air so that the air presses the car down onto the road. This downforce is what lets the car corner at speeds that feel impossible. The floor is so important that teams guard its shape like a secret, because the family of tricks that pulls the car toward the ground, known as ground effect, can be worth more lap time than the engine itself. The engine has changed too. Today's Formula 1 cars are hybrids, the same basic idea as a hybrid road car. When the driver brakes, the car captures energy that would normally be wasted as heat and stores it in a battery. A moment later, the driver can spend that stored energy for a burst of extra power. A racing team will fight for a hundredth of a second, so no scrap of energy is allowed to go to waste. Safety improved in step with speed, and often because of terrible lessons. Drivers now sit inside a carbon shell built to shatter in a crash and absorb the impact. They wear fireproof suits. A curved bar called the halo guards the head. Crashes that would once have been fatal are now often walked away from, and that progress was not an accident. It was designed, tested, and paid for over decades. The race track, in the end, is a laboratory moving at two hundred miles an hour.

blocks.prompt: The Fastest Laboratory on Earth
blocks.text: A Formula 1 car looks like a toy that has been stretched flat and given wings, but it is closer to a fighter jet than to anything in a driveway. It is the product of an old and strange bargain: teams spend enormous sums and take real risks to shave hundredths of a second off a lap, and in return the rest of us slowly inherit safer, smarter cars. To understand the machine, it helps to understand the single idea that shapes almost every part of it. That idea is downforce. An airplane wing is curved so that moving air lifts it into the sky. A race car turns that logic upside down. Its wings and its intricately shaped floor are built to push air upward, and by Newton's old rule that every action has an equal and opposite reaction, the air pushes the car down in return. At full speed the effect is staggering. A modern Formula 1 car generates more downforce than the car weighs, which means that, in principle, it could cling to the ceiling of a tunnel and drive along upside down. That invisible hand pressing the tires into the track is what allows the car to corner at speeds that would fling an ordinary vehicle into the barriers. Downforce, though, is only half the design. The other half is survival. Racing spent its first decades as one of the deadliest sports on Earth, and nearly every safety feature on the car today was born from a death that engineers refused to repeat. The driver sits inside a monocoque, a single molded tub of carbon fiber that is lighter than aluminum yet strong enough to stay whole while everything around it disintegrates. That disintegration is deliberate. The nose, the wings, and the wheels are designed to break away and carry the crash energy with them, so that less of it reaches the body inside. Above the driver's head arcs the halo, a titanium loop that was mocked as ugly when it appeared and has since stopped tires, walls, and flying debris from crushing the people it guards. Notice what the writer is doing across this passage. The wonder comes first, the danger second, and that order is a choice. We are invited to marvel at a car that could drive on a ceiling before we are reminded that people once died in these machines every season. The two halves are not separate stories. The same downforce that makes the cornering possible is exactly what makes a crash so violent, and so the pursuit of speed and the pursuit of safety are locked together, each one forcing the other forward. That is the real engine of the sport. Every hundredth of a second clawed back on the track pushes engineers to protect the driver a little better, and every life saved gives them the confidence to chase the next hundredth. The track is a laboratory, and the lessons written there in carbon and titanium eventually find their way, quietly, into the ordinary car waiting in your garage.
